newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Gilts see light beyond rate worries.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Gilts see light beyond rate worries.

text.p: British gilts should be able to weather the storm of any interest rate increase this week and still head higher in the medium term, analysts said on Wednesday.
In the near-term the British debt market would continue to cede ground to Bunds on spreads, but could clamber higher once interest rate worries had dissipated.
"If you look at where some of the other high yielders have come from...a couple of years ago Italy was 620 - now it's 93," said Jonathan York, broker at Mees Pierson Derivatives in London.
"There is no reason why gilts can't head for the same sort of level," he added.

But the gilt/Bund spread, now at 160 basis points, was unlikely to recapture the 130 levels seen after the May 1 election and subsequent independence of the Bank of England (BoE) just yet, analysts said.

Once a widely expected rate rise is out of the way the gilt market could benefit from any signs of tame inflation. Rampant consumer spending in past months has kindled inflation fears after what was considered to be a moderate budget by the new Labour government.
"With an independent central bank inflation fears shouldn't really be there, provided the Bank is prepared to jump on inflation at every opportunity," said York.

But investors would still have to weigh positive sentiment towards gilts against a possible string of rate rises by the newly independent BoE in the coming months to cool down the consumer sector, analysts said.
"The market is being pulled between two influences like a see-saw," said Glenn Davies, Chief UK economist at Credit Lyonnais in London.
"On the one hand there are base rate rise worries, on the other the feeling gilts are attractive compared to other (European) markets," he added.
A rate rise would buoy sterling further in currency markets, increasing the appeal of gilts for foreign investors, analysts said.
But according to Davies the base rate effect would eventually dominate, and the spread to Bunds widen.
By 1230 GMT, the September gilt future was little changed on the day, up 1/32 at 114-22. The 10-year gilt/Bund spread was 165, up five basis points from Tuesday.
"It's a little bit difficult to see the spread going as high as the 180 which we saw before the election," Davies said.
At that time, September gilt futures were trading at just above 108-00.
Analysts pointed the finger of blame at Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's July 2 budget for any near-term losses gilts could accrue.
Fresh evidence of simmering inflation was provided by this week's retail price index which showed a year-on-year rise of 2.7 percent in June, overshooting the government's 2.5 percent target.
"The budget failed in terms of rebalancing things in the way gilts would have liked to have seen," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale in London.
"Now the onus is back on interest rates," he added.
Still, the gilt/Bund spread could converge from both sides in the longer term. Bund yields were also likely to lose ground to gilts, analysts said.
Rayner at Societe Generale said fears Germany may struggle to meet the 3.0 percent budget deficit/GDP EMU target could help to squeeze the spread.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday set the 1998 budget spending at 461 billion marks, above an original target of 447 billion, due to high unemployment costs.
Despite a possible rate rise analysts expect curve flattening to resume soon.
"The problem is the yield curve is already incredibly flat," said Davies at Credit Lyonnais.
"It looks like for the gilt/Bund spread to remain at 160 with the base rates going up, the curve would actually have to invert."
-- International Bonds Unit = 44 171 542 8663
